word:greek-nt:G0046.explanation: This word means “unshrunk,” describing cloth that has not yet been reduced or tightened by shrinking. It is a descriptive word for the condition of material, especially when distinguishing new cloth from cloth that has already been treated or worn. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew 9:16 and Mark 2:21. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains cloth in an unshrunk state.

word:greek-nt:G0110.explanation: Athanasia means immortality—imperishability and freedom from death.

word:greek-nt:G0280.explanation: This word describes something that goes “beyond limits” or is “immoderate”—more than is properly measured or restrained. It points to excess rather than a balanced or fitting amount, and it functions as a description of going beyond an established boundary. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both in 2 Corinthians 10. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is clear: exceeding reasonable limits.

word:greek-nt:G0301.explanation: Amos is a personal name, referring to a man named in the genealogical records of the New Testament. It identifies an ancestor in Jesus’ recorded lineage, rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name appears three times in the Greek New Testament, in two verses: twice in Matthew 1:10 and once in Luke 3:25. Its precise significance in those passages comes from the surrounding genealogy, but its basic function is simply to identify the person called Amos.

word:greek-nt:G0437.explanation: This word means “to give thanks” or “to praise.” It describes expressing grateful acknowledgment toward God or another recipient, rather than merely feeling thankful inwardly. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 2:38, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains an outward response of gratitude or praise, directed toward the one being honored.

word:greek-nt:G0558.explanation: This word means “freedman,” referring to a person who has been released from slavery. It is a noun that identifies someone by a former condition of bondage and a present condition of freedom. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Corinthians 7:22. That reference marks its only recorded occurrence in this corpus; the word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding text.

word:greek-nt:G0705.explanation: Arithmeō means to count or number.

word:greek-nt:G0792.explanation: Aster means a star. Scripture uses it for a single star seen in the sky and for stars in the heavens.

word:greek-nt:G0932.explanation: Basileia means kingship, sovereignty, authority, or rule; it can also mean a kingdom, a concrete realm. Scripture speaks of entering God's Kingdom. Elsewhere, it describes a kingdom with no end.

word:greek-nt:G0969.explanation: Bēryllos means beryl, a precious stone that may have various colors, including sea-green.

word:greek-nt:G1074.explanation: Genea means a generation or generations. It is used for successive generations in a family line, and also for a generation characterized as evil or faithless.

word:greek-nt:G1117.explanation: This word means “cargo”: goods or merchandise being carried from one place to another. It refers to a load transported by ship or other means, rather than to the vessel itself or to the act of traveling. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in one verse in Acts and two verses in Revelation. Its exact emphasis in any one verse comes from the surrounding sentence and passage.

word:greek-nt:G1287.explanation: Diaskorpizō means to scatter. It can also describe wasting property.

word:greek-nt:G1355.explanation: Dioper means therefore or wherefore, emphatically connecting what came before with a resulting statement.

word:greek-nt:G1566.explanation: Ekeise means there, thither, or at that place.

word:greek-nt:G1588.explanation: This word describes those who are “elect” or “select”—those marked out as selected rather than treated as part of an undifferentiated group. Its central idea is distinction by selection, identifying people or things regarded as the selected ones. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 22 times, making it a recurring description rather than a term limited to one passage. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but “elect” and “select” express its basic meaning.

word:greek-nt:G1702.explanation: Empaizō means to mock or ridicule. It is used when people mocked someone by kneeling before him and calling him “King of the Jews.”

word:greek-nt:G1759.explanation: Enthen means here, in this place.

word:greek-nt:G1795.explanation: This word means “to be engraved” or “to engrave,” describing something marked or written firmly into a surface. Its basic picture is writing that is impressed so it remains inscribed rather than merely spoken or temporarily displayed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 3:7. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on engraving or being engraved.

word:greek-nt:G1841.explanation: Exodos means an exit, going out, or departure. It can also refer to death.

word:greek-nt:G1975.explanation: Epiporeuomai means to travel or journey, including coming to someone.

word:greek-nt:G2109.explanation: Euergeteo means to do good. It can also mean to benefit someone.

word:greek-nt:G2152.explanation: Eusebēs means pious, devout, or God-fearing.

word:greek-nt:G2318.explanation: Theosebēs means devout, pious, or God-fearing. It describes a worshiper of God who does his will.

word:greek-nt:G2354.explanation: Threneō means to lament, wail, or bewail.

word:greek-nt:G2383.explanation: Iairos is the personal name Jairus. Jairus is identified as a ruler of the synagogue.

word:greek-nt:G2404.explanation: This word refers to Hierapolis, a place-name mentioned once in the Greek New Testament. It is not a common description or action word, but the name of a specific location. The English Bible preserves it as “Hierapolis.” Its sole occurrence is in Colossians 4:13, while the precise significance of the place in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its actual context.

word:greek-nt:G2611.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “to bandage”: to cover and bind a wound with material so it can be cared for. It functions as a verb, describing an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 10:34. The word’s basic sense is practical and concrete, referring to the act of treating an injury rather than expressing an abstract idea.

word:greek-nt:G2743.explanation: This word means “to be seared as with a hot iron” or “to brand.” It describes something marked by burning, as skin may be permanently scarred or branded. The image emphasizes a visible, lasting mark rather than a temporary impression. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 4:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage, but the word itself points to being burned so as to leave a lasting mark.

word:greek-nt:G2794.explanation: Kindynos means danger or peril. It names dangers encountered on journeys, from robbers, and in the wilderness.

word:greek-nt:G2857.explanation: Kolossai names the town of Colossae.

word:greek-nt:G2970.explanation: Kōmos means reveling. It can also refer to an orgy.

word:greek-nt:G3090.explanation: Lois is the name of Timothy’s grandmother.

word:greek-nt:G3128.explanation: Manassēs is the personal name Manasseh. It refers to Hezekiah’s son in one context and to an Israelite tribe in another.

word:greek-nt:G3164.explanation: Machomai means to fight. It can also mean to contend or quarrel.

word:greek-nt:G3335.explanation: Metalambanō means to share in or partake of something.

word:greek-nt:G3573.explanation: Nystazō means to become drowsy, doze, or slumber.

word:greek-nt:G3685.explanation: This word expresses the desire to receive benefit or experience joy from someone or something. Its two closely related meanings are “to have benefit” and “to have joy,” so it can describe a hoped-for good result or gladness received. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Philemon 1:20. The surrounding verse is needed to determine whether the emphasis there falls more on receiving help or on the joy that comes from it.

word:greek-nt:G3803.explanation: Pagis means a snare or trap. It can also describe a stratagem or device that ensnares people.

word:greek-nt:G3876.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “disobedience”: failure or refusal to obey what has been commanded. As a noun, it names the act or condition of not obeying, rather than describing the command itself. It appears three times in the Greek New Testament, and each occurrence is rendered “disobedience.” Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a departure from obedience to an authority or instruction.

word:greek-nt:G3898.explanation: This word means “in just the same way” or “similarly.” It is an adverb that connects an action or statement with something already mentioned, showing that the two are alike in manner. It describes how something happens rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 2:14. Its basic sense is to mark likeness or correspondence, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being compared.

word:greek-nt:G3951.explanation: This word means “to incite”: it describes stirring someone or a group to action, often by urging them on. As a verb, it points to causing a response rather than merely describing a feeling or opinion. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 13:50. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is causing others to act.

word:greek-nt:G4006.explanation: Pepoithēsis means confidence, trust, or reliance.

word:greek-nt:G4073.explanation: Petra means a rock. It can also refer to stony ground, as when seed fell on rock and withered for lack of moisture.

word:greek-nt:G4312.explanation: Propeteis means impulsive, rash, or reckless.

word:greek-nt:G4349.explanation: This word means “stumbling” or “stumbling block”—something associated with tripping or causing someone to stumble. It can describe an obstacle that interferes with a person’s progress rather than a physical act alone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 6:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is an impediment or cause of stumbling.

word:greek-nt:G4385.explanation: Proteino means to stretch out. It can also describe being tied up for scourging.

word:greek-nt:G4428.explanation: This word means “to roll up,” describing the action of gathering or folding something into a rolled form. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 4:20. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s exact object and significance in that scene cannot be stated safely. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: something is rolled up rather than left spread out or unfolded.

word:greek-nt:G4464.explanation: Rhabdos means a rod or staff. It can also mean a scepter or a rod associated with rule.

word:greek-nt:G4590.explanation: Shem is the name of a son of Noah.

word:greek-nt:G4635.explanation: This word refers to a tentmaker, a person who makes tents. It is a noun describing someone by this occupation, rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Acts 18:3. The word’s basic meaning remains focused and concrete: a worker whose trade is making tents. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies the person’s occupation.

word:greek-nt:G4727.explanation: Stenazō means to groan. It can express desire, as when people groan while longing for what is from heaven.

word:greek-nt:G4819.explanation: Symbainō means to happen or occur.

word:greek-nt:G4842.explanation: Sympempō means to send together with someone.

word:greek-nt:G4907.explanation: Synesis means understanding. It can also mean practical discernment. It is used for understanding a mystery and where hearers are amazed at a person's understanding and answers.

word:greek-nt:G5034.explanation: Tachos means quickness or speed, describing an action done quickly.

word:greek-nt:G5078.explanation: Technē means skill or craft. It can also refer to a trade. It can describe art used in engraving.

word:greek-nt:G5096.explanation: Timon is a personal name belonging to one of the seven original deacons chosen in Jerusalem.

word:greek-nt:G5171.explanation: This word means “to live in luxury” or “to self-indulge.” It describes a person enjoying excessive comfort and pleasure rather than practicing restraint. As a verb, it portrays an active lifestyle of indulgence, not merely possessing wealth or receiving a benefit. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 5:5. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on luxurious, self-satisfying living.

word:greek-nt:G5232.explanation: Hyperauxanō means to increase exceedingly or beyond measure.

word:greek-nt:G5269.explanation: This word means “to undergird,” describing the action of strengthening or supporting something from beneath. It functions as an action word: it points to taking measures that help hold something together or keep it secure. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:17, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word’s central idea is practical support that provides stability.

word:greek-nt:G5467.explanation: Chalepos means hard or troublesome, and can also mean harsh or fierce. It describes people whose fierceness made the way impassable.

word:greek-nt:G5562.explanation: Chōreō means to make room for or contain. It can also mean to go or receive.
